prompt: Your compose file has worked on every laptop on the team for months. A new hire clones the repo and runs `docker compose up`. What breaks first for them, and why did it not break for anyone else?

criteria: Names something the stack needs that lives outside the file, such as a .env file or a local secret
Explains that existing machines already carry state from setup steps nobody repeats
Says the fresh clone is the only honest test of whether the file is complete
Gives a fix, such as committing an example env file or folding the step into the compose file

prompt: A project's compose file starts the API and the database, and the README adds: "then run the migration script by hand, then load the seed rows from the wiki page." Critique that arrangement.

criteria: Says the two manual steps belong in the compose file or a scripted entrypoint
Names the wiki as a place the seed data will drift out of step with the schema
Points out the stack cannot come up without a person reading prose first
Notes the database has to be accepting connections before the migration can run

prompt: Match each compose key to the thing it is actually responsible for.

right: Starts one service only after another has been started
Keeps data alive when a container is destroyed and recreated
Gives other services a readiness signal to wait on, not just a start signal
Passes configuration into the container at run time

prompt: This stack comes up with no errors, but the API cannot reach the database. Exactly one line is wrong — which?

answer.why: Inside the api container, `localhost` is the api container itself. Compose puts both services on a shared network where each is reachable by its service name, so the host has to be `db`.

prompt: A production bug gets fixed by shelling into the running container and patching the file in place. It works, the alert clears, and everyone goes home. What breaks first?

criteria: Says the fix is gone at the next restart or redeploy
Notes that the running container no longer matches its image
Points out that other replicas never received the patch
Names the source repository as now out of step with production

prompt: A colleague shells into a running container, edits a config file, and announces "I changed the image." Explain why that sentence is wrong.

criteria: States that the edit landed in the container's writable layer
Says the image itself is fixed once it has been built
Notes the edit disappears when the container is replaced
Names rebuilding from the Dockerfile as the way to change an image

prompt: You run `docker run` three times against the same tag, and all three processes are still up. How many images and how many containers now exist?

options: One image, one container
Three images, three containers
One image, three containers
Three images, one container

prompt: Which of these hold true about how an image relates to a container?

options: Many containers can run from a single image at the same time
Removing a container also removes the image it was started from
A container puts a writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers
Two containers started from one image begin with identical file contents
Each container has to be built from an image of its own

prompt: You change one character in a source file and your image takes eight minutes to rebuild. A colleague makes the same size change to a service on the same base image and theirs is back in twelve seconds. Explain what is different about the two Dockerfiles.

criteria: States that each instruction produces a layer that can be reused from cache
States that a changed layer invalidates every layer after it
Identifies copying the source before installing dependencies as the cause of the slow build
Names the fix: copy the dependency manifest, install, then copy the rest of the source

prompt: A Dockerfile copies the whole project directory and then runs `pip install -r requirements.txt`. You edit only `README.md` and rebuild. What happens?

options: Every layer hits the cache, so only image metadata is rewritten
The copy layer is invalidated and pip reinstalls every dependency from scratch
Docker notices the requirements file is unchanged and reuses the install layer
pip finds its own download cache in the image and skips the install

prompt: Put these Dockerfile instructions in the order that keeps a dependency install out of the path of everyday source changes.
When is putting `COPY . .` near the top of a Dockerfile not worth arguing about?

criteria: Gives a case where nothing expensive runs after the copy step
Notes that the ordering only pays off when the following step is slow
Mentions a build that starts with no cache to reuse, such as a fresh runner, gains nothing either way
States that the careful ordering costs nothing, so it stays the default

prompt: Everything a container writes goes into its own layer, which is discarded the moment the container is ______. To keep database files past that, you mount a ______ over the directory the database writes to.
A colleague's local Postgres setup declares no volumes at all. They insist it is fine — they start it every morning and last week's rows are always still there. Critique their reasoning.

criteria: States that the rows are sitting in the container's writable layer
Distinguishes stopping a container from removing one
Names a concrete event that wipes it, such as a down or an image bump
Recommends a named volume mounted at the data directory

prompt: This Compose file is meant to keep the database's data across a `docker compose down`. It runs without error, and the volume shows up in `docker volume ls`, but the data is gone after a down and up. Find the line at fault.

answer.why: Postgres writes to /var/lib/postgresql/data, not /var/lib/postgres/data. The volume mounts one path off, so it stays empty while the real data files land in the container's writable layer and vanish with the container.

prompt: Mounting a host directory straight into a container is the usual first move. Name a situation where you would not do it, and say what you would reach for instead.

criteria: Names a specific situation rather than a general worry
Gives a reason tied to permissions, host paths, or portability
Names named volumes or a managed store as the replacement
Concedes at least one case where a host mount is the right tool

prompt: A scheduled job has been quietly writing bad rows for two hours. Put these steps in the order a first responder should take them.

items: Work out which code change introduced the bug
Stop the job from firing again on its next schedule
Backfill the two hours of bad rows once a fix has shipped
Confirm the output really is wrong and not a stale dashboard cache
Tell the people reading the affected numbers not to trust them

prompt: The pipeline has been failing for forty minutes. A senior engineer on the call wants to keep reading logs until the root cause is found before anyone touches the deployment. Push back.

criteria: Argues for restoring service first, such as rolling back to the last release that worked
Says the cause can still be found afterwards from logs and artefacts kept aside
Names what is being lost for every further minute of searching
Concedes a case where continuing to investigate wins, such as a rollback that is unsafe to run

prompt: Eight minutes ago the nightly load finished with half the rows it normally writes, and the morning dashboards are already showing the gap. You do not know why yet. Write the first message you post in the channel the business owners are watching.

criteria: Opens with what is wrong for the reader, such as which numbers are unreliable
States the affected time window, not only the symptom right now
Says what people should avoid doing or trusting in the meantime
Commits to a time for the next update rather than to a fix time
Names no cause that has not been confirmed yet

prompt: A shell script runs end to end from your terminal. You paste the identical command into `crontab -e`, and every night at 02:00 it fails leaving no output anywhere. What breaks first, and how would you prove it?

criteria: Names the environment difference, such as a PATH that is not the one from your shell
Says your shell profile and its exports are never sourced for a cron job
Mentions the working directory being the home directory rather than the project
Gives a concrete check, such as running `env` from cron or redirecting both streams to a log file

prompt: When does the schedule `*/10 2 * * *` actually fire?

options: Every ten minutes, around the clock
Every ten minutes from 02:00 to 02:50, once a day
At 02:10, once a day
Every ten hours, starting at 02:00

prompt: One line in this crontab cannot do what its author intended. Which one, and why?

answer.why: cron reads an unescaped `%` as a newline: the command is cut off after `date +` and everything past it is handed to the job on stdin. Each percent sign has to be written `\%`, or the date has to be computed inside the script instead.

prompt: Someone wants to schedule a forty-minute data load with cron, running every thirty minutes. When is cron the wrong tool for a job, and what would you reach for instead?

criteria: Points out that runs overlap because cron never waits for the previous one to finish
Names what cron does not give you, such as retries, alerting on failure, or dependencies between jobs
Offers a minimum fix such as a lock file or `flock` to prevent overlap
Names an alternative with run history and dependency handling

prompt: A colleague's loader opens `config/settings.yml` and has never failed when they run it by hand from their project folder. Scheduled in cron, it dies on the first night. What breaks first, and why did the manual run hide it?

criteria: States that the path is resolved against the working directory
Says cron starts the job somewhere else, often the home directory
Names an absolute path or an explicit cd as the fix
Explains that the manual run happened to start in the right place

prompt: You SSH into a server you have never touched before and a nightly job is failing. Name the first three places you look on the filesystem and say what each one tells you.

criteria: Names /var/log or a service log path as one of the three
Says what /etc holds and why config is checked before code
Gives a reason for each location rather than listing paths alone
Mentions checking free space or a full filesystem as a cause

prompt: Match each directory on an unfamiliar Linux box to what you would expect to find there.

right: The record of what a job did the last time it ran
Scratch space that may be wiped on reboot
Executables placed there by the package manager
One person's own files and dotfiles

prompt: A script runs `cd /srv/reports`, then `cd ../etl`, then `pwd`. What does `pwd` print?

options: /srv/etl
/srv/reports/etl
/etl
/srv

prompt: A file listed as `-rw-r-----` is owned by user `alice` and group `analysts`. A member of `analysts` who is not alice may ____ the file but may not ____ it.
A deploy script ends with the line `chmod -R 777 /srv/app/uploads`, under a comment reading "fixes permission errors". Critique that line.

criteria: States that 777 makes the tree writable by every local account
Says the real question is which user the service runs as
Names chown plus a narrower mode such as 750 as the fix
Points out that -R also marks every file below as executable

prompt: A contractor messages you: "I keep getting Permission denied writing to the shared export folder — just put me in sudo and I'll stop bothering you." Write your reply.

criteria: Names group membership or directory ownership as the smaller fix
States that sudo grants the whole machine, not one folder
Asks for the exact path and the error text before changing anything
Offers a concrete next step instead of a flat no

prompt: This provisioning snippet sets up a service account and its credentials. Exactly one line is a real security bug — which one?

answer.why: The directory holding the database credentials is left writable by every account on the box. The 600 mode on the last line protects the contents of db.conf, but a world-writable parent directory lets any local user delete that entry and drop in their own file, which the service will then read. This directory wants chmod 700.

prompt: A nightly wrapper script has `python load.py` on one line and `echo "load complete"` on the next, and the scheduler has reported success every morning for a year. Critique it.

criteria: States that the script exits with the status of `echo`, which is always zero
Says the scheduler therefore records success on nights when the load failed
Names a fix such as `set -e`, or testing `$?` straight after the python call
Points out that a line printed on stdout is not evidence the step did anything

prompt: Match each exit status a job reports to what actually happened to the process.

right: Killed by SIGKILL — often the out-of-memory killer rather than a person
The command was never found on PATH, so nothing ran at all
Ran to completion and reported no failure
Interrupted from the terminal with Ctrl-C

prompt: A bash script with no `set -o pipefail` runs `cat missing_file.csv | wc -l` and then `echo $?`. What does that second line print, and why does it matter to a scheduler?

accept: 0 - the pipeline reports wc's status, not cat's
0, so the scheduler sees success even though cat failed
answer.explain: A pipeline exits with the status of its last command. `cat` fails with 1 and writes to stderr, but `wc -l` succeeds on the empty stream, so the line reports 0 and any scheduler watching the exit code records a clean run. `set -o pipefail` makes the pipeline return the rightmost non-zero status instead.

prompt: A deploy script sends SIGKILL to a worker because SIGTERM had not stopped it two seconds later. When is skipping straight to SIGKILL the right move, and what are you giving up by not waiting?

criteria: States that SIGKILL cannot be caught, blocked, or handled by the process
Names cleanup the process now skips, such as flushing a buffer or releasing a lock or lease
Says two seconds is short for a worker still finishing an in-flight task
Gives a case where SIGKILL is the answer, such as a process that ignores SIGTERM or is wedged in uninterruptible work

prompt: A team keeps one private key file in the shared password manager, and every new hire downloads that file to get onto the servers. Critique the arrangement.

criteria: States that a shared private key destroys per-person attribution
Says revoking one leaver's access means rotating it for everyone
Names one key pair per person as the alternative
Notes that the key now exists on every machine anyone copied it to

prompt: Which of these statements about an SSH key pair hold up?

options: The public half is what gets copied onto each server you want to reach
If you lose the private half you can regenerate it from the public half
A passphrase on the private key limits the damage if the laptop is stolen
During the handshake the server proves it holds your private key
One key pair can authorise you on any number of unrelated servers

prompt: True or false: an attacker who obtains a copy of the `authorized_keys` file from a server can use it to log in as that user. Justify the verdict.

criteria: States that authorized_keys contains public keys only
Says login requires the matching private key, which the file lacks
Describes the client signing a challenge to prove possession
Notes that write access to that file would be the real danger
States that authorized_keys contains public keys only
Says login requires the matching private key, which the file lacks
Describes the client signing a challenge to prove possession
Notes that write access to that file would be the real danger

prompt: A client's office manager emails: "Please send over your SSH key so IT can set up your access." Write the reply you would actually send.

criteria: Sends the public key and names the .pub file explicitly
States that the private half never leaves your machine
Explains the reason in one line without a lecture on cryptography
Ends with a concrete next step or a question about where to send it

prompt: Two copies of the same worker get started on one box — one from a systemd unit, one from a tmux session someone left running — and both are configured to listen on port 9000. What breaks first, and what does the copy that survives see?

criteria: States that only one process can hold the listening socket
Says the second start fails with address already in use
Notes that the first listener keeps serving traffic untouched
Points out the surviving process shows no sign of the conflict

prompt: An app on a server is bound to `127.0.0.1:8080`. Logged into that server, `curl localhost:8080` returns a page, but a load balancer on another host times out. What is going on?

options: Another process has already taken port 8080
The listener accepts connections only over the loopback interface
The load balancer has to authenticate before it can connect
Port 8080 is reserved and cannot be reached from off the host

prompt: A service refuses to start with "address already in use" on a box several teams share. Order the steps for tracking it down.

items: Restart the service and confirm it is listening where you expect
Read the error to get the exact address and port it wanted
Decide whether the process holding the port should be running at all
Run `ss -ltnp` to find which process currently holds it
Stop that process or move the new service to a different port

prompt: Binding a service to 0.0.0.0 is the default in most tutorials. Name the cases where it is the wrong choice, and say what you would bind to instead.

criteria: States that 0.0.0.0 accepts connections on every interface
Names a database, admin panel or metrics port as a case to keep local
Gives 127.0.0.1 as the bind address for same-host callers
Mentions a proxy or an SSH tunnel as how remote callers still reach it

prompt: Leadership asks how long it would take to have the warehouse serving queries again if the primary cluster vanished this morning. Give your estimate and show how you got there.

criteria: Gives a range rather than a single confident number
Splits the number into provision, restore, replay and verify
Names what the estimate hangs on, such as data volume or archive location
States that the figure is a guess until a drill measures it

prompt: Your manager points out that the nightly snapshot job has exited green for 400 days straight, so spending a sprint day on a restore rehearsal is hard to justify. Respond.

criteria: Separates the job exiting zero from the archive being usable
Names one failure a green job would never catch
Proposes a time-boxed drill rather than an open-ended project
Asks what recovery time the business is actually assuming

prompt: This cron script has been reporting success every night for a year. Exactly one line is why the backups may be worthless — which one?

answer.why: A shell pipeline reports the exit status of its last command, so `set -e` sees gzip succeed even when pg_dump dies partway. The script writes a perfectly valid gzip file containing a truncated dump, exits zero, and the next line then deletes the older archives that were still restorable. Add `set -o pipefail`, or dump to a file and check the status before compressing.

prompt: True or false: a backup job that has reported success every night for a year is evidence that you can restore from it. Justify the verdict.

criteria: Distinguishes the job finishing from the data coming back
Names something a green job misses, such as a truncated or unreadable archive
States that only a performed restore counts as evidence
Says the drill has to produce a measured elapsed time
Distinguishes the job finishing from the data coming back
Names something a green job misses, such as a truncated or unreadable archive
States that only a performed restore counts as evidence
Says the drill has to produce a measured elapsed time

prompt: A four-person team keeps the warehouse password in a `config.yaml` that lives in the repo, reasoning that the repo is private. Two years later the team is thirty people plus rotating contractors. What breaks first?

criteria: Names the widening set of people with read access as the failure
Says the value stays in git history even after someone edits the file
Points out that nobody can tell who has already copied it out
Proposes an environment variable or a secret store as the replacement

prompt: You find a live cloud access key in a commit that was pushed to the shared remote yesterday. What is the first thing you do?

options: Rotate the key at the provider and load the replacement from the secret store
Force-push a rewritten history so the commit no longer exists
Add the file to `.gitignore` and commit that change
File a ticket so the cleanup can be planned into the next sprint

prompt: A database password has been sitting in the repository's git history for months. Put these four steps in the order you would carry them out.

items: Revoke the exposed credential at the provider
Issue a replacement credential and put it in the secret store
Purge the value from git history and tell clone holders to re-clone
Redeploy the services so they read the replacement

prompt: A manager asks why an engineer lost most of a day after a coworker pasted an API key into a commit and deleted it an hour later. Write what you tell the manager, without jargon.

criteria: States that the key had to be replaced, not just removed from the file
Explains that the old commit survives in history and in every clone
Says the exposed key kept working until someone revoked it
Avoids implying that deleting the line undid the exposure
